{{Short description|Theorem in complex analysis}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Hartogs–Rosenthal theorem''' is a classical result in [[complex analysis]] on the [[uniform approximation]] of continuous functions on compact subsets of the [[complex plane]] by [[rational function]]s. The theorem was proved in 1931 by the German mathematicians [[Friedrich Hartogs]] and [[Arthur Rosenthal]] and has been widely applied, particularly in [[operator theory]].

==Statement==
The Hartogs–Rosenthal theorem states that if ''K'' is a compact subset of the complex plane with [[Lebesgue measure]] zero, then any continuous complex-valued function on ''K'' can be uniformly approximated by rational functions.

==Proof==
By the [[Stone–Weierstrass theorem]] any complex-valued continuous function on ''K'' can be uniformly approximated by a polynomial in <math>z</math> and <math>\overline{z}</math>.

So it suffices to show that <math>\overline{z}</math> can be uniformly approximated by a rational function on ''K''.

Let ''g(z)'' be a [[smooth function]] of compact support on '''C''' equal to 1 on ''K'' and set

:<math> f(z)=g(z)\cdot \overline{z}.</math>

By the [[Cauchy_integral_formula#Smooth_functions|generalized Cauchy integral formula]]

:<math>f(z) =  \frac{1}{2\pi i}\iint_{{C\backslash K}} \frac{\partial f}{\partial \bar{w}}\frac{dw\wedge d\bar{w}}{w-z}, </math>

since ''K'' has measure zero.

Restricting ''z'' to ''K'' and taking [[Riemann sum|Riemann approximating sums]] for the integral on the right hand side yields the required uniform approximation of <math>\bar{z}</math> by a rational function.<ref>{{harvnb|Conway|2000}}</ref>
